## Three outputs from gradient boosting {#sec-xgb-model}

A forecast needs a probability of positive burned area and a model for its magnitude.
XGBoostLSS [@maerz2022xgboostlss] connects the tree-building machinery of XGBoost to a
distributional loss. Its name means *location, scale and shape*: the model learns a
score for each parameter of the chosen distribution.

Here three scores describe the [hurdle Beta](index.qmd#sec-likelihood). Two become the
Beta concentrations, $\alpha>0$ and $\beta>0$; the third becomes the zero probability
$\pi\in(0,1)$. The quantities we report are

$$
p_{\mathrm{occ}}=1-\pi,\qquad
\mu=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},\qquad
\phi=\alpha+\beta,\qquad
\widehat E[Y]=p_{\mathrm{occ}}\mu.
$$

$\mu$ describes the positive fraction; $\widehat E[Y]$ includes the chance of a zero.
These answer different questions, especially in counties with infrequent detections.

### How the loss grows trees

At boosting round $r$, the model updates its three unconstrained scores:

$$
\boldsymbol\eta^{(r)}(x)
=\boldsymbol\eta^{(r-1)}(x)+\nu\boldsymbol f^{(r)}(x).
$$

The learning rate $\nu$ scales the update. Gradients and Hessians of the negative
log-likelihood determine the tree splits and leaf values. Separate trees update the
three parameters; the implementation does not use cross-parameter Hessian blocks.
Its L2 derivative stabilization rescales the parameter updates before tree fitting.

Response functions keep the parameters inside their domains. The first concentration
uses a softplus, the second a scaled sigmoid with a cap, and the gate a sigmoid.
The concentration cap and maximum leaf update constrain numerical behavior. They are
part of this implementation and belong in its recorded configuration.

### Give exact zeros their own probability {#sec-xgb-hurdle}

For a zero response, the likelihood contribution is $\pi$. For a positive response,
it is $(1-\pi)\operatorname{Beta}(y;\alpha,\beta)$. Adding a density evaluated near
zero to the gate would mix a probability mass and a continuous density.

The custom distribution implements the two branches directly:

~~~python
def log_prob(self, value):
    is_zero = value == 0
    safe_value = torch.where(is_zero, torch.full_like(value, 0.5), value)
    return torch.where(
        is_zero,
        torch.log(self.gate),
        torch.log1p(-self.gate) + self.base_dist.log_prob(safe_value),
    )
~~~

The dummy value $0.5$ prevents an unused $\log(0)$ calculation from producing
invalid gradients. Positive observations retain their exact recorded values.
The search and fit both use this likelihood.

## One row for each county, origin, and horizon {#sec-xgb-horizon}

This is a direct multi-horizon model. The lead time is a feature, so one
booster learns the twelve forecasts issued at each origin. Each response window
belongs wholly to train, test, or validation. The lookback is 48 months and the
forecast horizon is 12 months.

The inputs are deliberately compact:

| Input | When it is known |
|---|---|
| Elevation, slope, sine and cosine of aspect | Fixed county terrain |
| Target-month calendar harmonics and horizon | Known at issuance |
| Burned fraction, occurrence, lags, rolling summaries | At or before the origin |
| Neighbor summaries of burned-area history | At or before the origin |
| Expanding county response summaries | Strictly before the origin |

County adjacency supplies the geography for neighbor summaries. The land-cover
category is held constant and carries no environmental information. No annual,
epoch, or observed target-month environmental measurements enter this fit.
The [data chapter](data.qmd) describes the retained response and its limitations.

### Keep every history index inside the past

A lagged response must satisfy $0\leq\text{index}\leq o$, where $o$ is the origin.
The lower bound matters because a negative Python index wraps to the end of an array.
The feature builder checks the available lookback against the largest requested lag.

County means also need an origin boundary. A county's full-training response mean
would contain outcomes that were still in the future at early training origins.
These fits instead use the expanding mean and occurrence rate strictly before each
origin. A later rolling forecast can use observations that have arrived since an
earlier forecast, while the fitted booster stays fixed.

## Fit on train, choose on test

The search uses the test split to choose hyperparameters and boosting duration.
Consequently its test score is a development score. The recorded search budget is
limited, so the selected configuration is an example of this procedure, not an
established optimum for the model class.

The selected fit is then used unchanged to predict train, test, and validation.
The saved configuration records the restricted forecast mode, feature names,
lookback, horizon, links, and boosting settings. The results generator verifies
forecast keys and targets against the canonical split files and recomputes its
scores from the saved parameters.

<!-- BEGIN FORECAST MODEL RESULTS -->
The completed search contains 12 trials, of which 12 completed with finite test NLL. Trial 7 supplied the selected fit.

The fit retains 482 boosting rounds, 2 spatial shell(s), 7 additional temporal lag(s), and 5 calendar harmonic pair(s).

The [result manifest](assets/forecast/summary.json) records the complete configuration, selection evidence, and source hashes.
<!-- END FORECAST MODEL RESULTS -->

The [Comparison chapter](comparison.qmd) brings together both models' train/test
scores, residual diagnostics, training G1 STACF heatmaps, and occurrence ROC and
precision–recall curves. All scores are recomputed from saved parameters after
checking complete forecast keys and outcomes. Validation results appear afterwards
in [Discussion](discussion.qmd).

## What these outputs establish

The booster supplies a fitted hurdle distribution for each requested horizon.
The positive mean, occurrence probability, and expected fraction are deterministic
outputs of one fitted model. Scores describe those outputs on the recorded forecast
requests; repeated horizons do not create independent observations.

These separate marginals do not specify a joint multi-month trajectory.
